title: Aminah at Abwa
hook: his mother dies on the road home from Yathrib when he is six

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zamzam's water washed the heart. Your line was: a washed heart. When you washed your hands slowly, what did you set down with the water? Day seven hundred nine.

A grown man stops at a grave and weeps, and the people with him weep too. Sahih Muslim keeps the scene. The man is the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the grave belongs to his mother. He was a small boy the last time he saw her alive. It happened far from home, on a journey, in a place called Abwa, on the road between Yathrib and Mecca. Today: Aminah.
screen: `A GRAVE BY THE ROAD.` → `A GROWN MAN WEEPS.` → `HIS MOTHER'S GRAVE.`

segments.voice: After the boy came back from Halimah's people, he lived with his mother, Aminah, in Mecca. The sirah says that when he was six, she took him north to Yathrib, the oasis town that would one day be called Medina, to visit relatives there. With them, the sirah says, went Umm Ayman, a woman of the household who helped care for him. On the way home, at Abwa, Aminah fell ill and died. She was buried there. And Umm Ayman brought the boy the rest of the way to Mecca without her. Sit with that road for a moment. His father, Abdullah, had died before he was born, the sirah says. He never saw his father's face. Now he has seen his mother's for the last time. That's the line for today: an orphan twice. Ibn Ishaq tells it in a few plain sentences, and doesn't dwell. It's the hadith from much later that shows how deep it went. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet visits his mother's grave and weeps, and he tells the people with him that he asked his Lord for permission to visit it, and permission was given. Then he says: visit graves, because they remind you of death. So the grief that began on a road at Abwa becomes, years later, a teaching about remembering. Notice who carried him home. Umm Ayman stays in the story, and Muslims remember her with honor. A loss, and right beside it, a woman who did not let go of his hand.
screen: `A JOURNEY NORTH TO YATHRIB.` · `ILLNESS AND DEATH AT ABWA.` · `UMM AYMAN BRINGS HIM HOME.` · `THE GROWN MAN AT THE GRAVE.` · then, large: `AN ORPHAN TWICE.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember a mother who died young. It may be your own mother, or a friend's, or someone you only heard about, or a woman in a story. Settle, and breathe. Bring her to mind, and the child she left behind. Hold them both, gently, without needing to fix anything. If this is too close today, remember Aminah instead, on the road at Abwa. At news of a death, Muslims say a line from surah two, which Pickthall renders: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." If you pray, you can say it now. If not, just keep her in mind. The bell holds the time.
screen: `LO! WE ARE ALLAH'S AND LO! UNTO HIM WE ARE RETURNING.`

segments.voice: Aminah. The Prophet's mother, who died on the road home from Yathrib, the sirah says, and was buried at Abwa while her small son was carried on to Mecca. Today's word.
Your line: an orphan twice. Today, think of one person who has lost a parent, and send them a short, kind word, or simply say their parent's name to them. Day seven hundred nine.

howItsDone: Muslims who hear of a death say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, from surah 2:156, and visiting graves to remember death follows the Prophet's ﷺ words in Sahih Muslim.

what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq tells the death briefly; Sahih Muslim gives the grown man weeping at the grave and the command to visit graves.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 976 (the Prophet visits his mother's grave and weeps; visit graves, they remind you of death)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Aminah's journey to Yathrib, her death at Abwa when he was six)
Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kabir (Umm Ayman on the journey; she brings the boy home to Mecca)

notes: The age six is stated only as the sirah's ('the sirah says'), per Ibn Ishaq. Confirm.
Umm Ayman's presence on the journey and her bringing him home: Ibn Sa'd and later sirah works; Ibn Ishaq's own text may not name her. Confirm the source and adjust the citation.

Sahih Muslim 976 also records that he asked permission to seek forgiveness for his mother and was not granted it. The script omits this theologically sensitive part and keeps only the visit, the weeping and the command to visit graves. A Keeper should decide whether the omission is acceptable or whether to address it.
'The Prophet kept her close all his life, the sources say' (Umm Ayman): confirm the hadith/sirah basis.
Pickthall 2:156 quoted from memory; confirm wording and capitalization.
The relatives in Yathrib are left unnamed (sirah: the Banu 'Adi ibn al-Najjar, maternal kin of Abd al-Muttalib).
